newsitem.title: RUSSIA: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN PLAYERS ESCAPE WEST IN SEARCH OF BETTER LIFE.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN PLAYERS ESCAPE WEST IN SEARCH OF BETTER LIFE.

text.p: Political and economic changes have reduced the former Soviet Union from a ice hockey power to a purveyor of world-class players for North American teams.
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 not only gave players more freedom to go abroad but prompted a crime wave and a slide in living conditions in Russia which many are only too happy to escape.
But although playing standards at home have slipped and crowds dwindled, steps are being taken to try to try and restore the glories and triumphs of the past.

"Our basis is strong and we prepare a lot of fine young players but as soon as they reach 19 they all go to the NHL (National Hockey League)," said Valentin Sych, president of the Russian Hockey Federation.
"A lot of good players and coaches are leaving because of the poor financial and social situation here. The ones left are those in whom the West has no interest."
About 520 Russians are now playing abroad, from Poland and Slovenia to Canada and the United States.
"Some Russian clubs may even offer good money to top players, but they do not want to stay because of the criminal situation here," Sych said.

A sports historian with Russia's Olympics Committee said many sportsmen were scared by organised crime, the plague of modern Russia. Mafia-style gangs, often employing former sportsmen, are reportedly extorting money from sportsmen.
"The mafia has made the sports business one of its sources of revenue. Bribes, extortion and killings are common. It is often not safe to practise sports here," said the historian.

Hundreds of fine players emerged from the Soviet cradle for more than 50 years. They were offered good training conditions from childhood, some won fame and some money. What they did not have was freedom to leave their clubs.

"The guys were really happy then. They were above the misery in which the country lived. They did not have to live in communal flats, queue for sausages or toilet paper. They could even travel abroad for a while," said the historian.

Those players led the Soviet Union, where professional sports was not officially recognised, to some memorable triumphs: the 1954 World Championship, gold at the 1956 Olympics, the 1979 Challenge Cup against the NHL and the Canada Cup of 1981.

"They were good times. The quality of hockey was really high and even big disappointments, such as third place at the 1977 World Championship and defeat by the United States at the 1980 Olympics, were exceptions caused by us overestimating our own capabilities," Sych said.

But with the first signs of democracy in the late 1980s, even before the break-up of the Soviet Union, a number of fine players struck deals with the NHL and left their clubs, to the astonishment of coaches and Communist Party bosses alike.
They were refused entry back into the Soviet Union and were attacked by the media but served as an example to hundreds of players who left as soon as the superpower broke up.

The legend of Soviet hockey lives on with players such as Vancouver Canucks' Alexander Mogilny and "Russian Rocket" Pavel Bure, Detroit Red Wings' Sergei Fyodorov and Vyacheslav Fetisov, Vladimir Tsyplakov of Los Angeles Kings and Alexei Kovalyov of the New York Rangers.

"People here have mixed feelings about Russians playing abroad. They are proud that they play in the best teams and score," Sych said. "But there is a lot of disappointment. As a hockey fan I would love to see them here, in Russian clubs."
Sych said standards in the Russian championship were now far below those of Soviet times, when Moscow teams such as CSKA, Spartak and Dinamo were a match for top North American teams.
Moves are afoot to improve standards. The number of teams competing in the domestic championship will be reduced from 26 to 24 next season and then to 22.
"We simply do not have enough high-class teams for that anymore," Sych said. "If you pour water in your borshch (traditional beetroot soup) it won't be tasty."
The number of spectators has also dropped but Sych still lives in hope.
"Our hockey is going through hard times, but it does not mean that there is no way out. Russia will overcome its difficulties, and our hockey will rise again," Sych said.

One source of hope is that Russian ice hockey teams are still competitive in Europe. Lada Togliatti won the European Cup late last year, and Dinamo Moscow finished second in the European League Championship last month.
Lada became the first team from outside Moscow to win Russia's Inter-regional Hockey League Cup in 1994, ending a four-year reign by Dinamo Moscow.
Lada rose to fame at the start of the 1990s under coach Gennady Tsygurov. But the team, from a town on the Volga River which is home to Russia's biggest car plant, is an exception.
"The whole car plant, the whole city is working for the sake of the team. Basically, they have everything a good team would need, here or in the West," said the Olympics Committee sports historian.
"Lada's players are good and refuse to go abroad if they are offered to play in a second-tier team like Switzerland. But even they cannot turn down an NHL contract."
One once great Moscow team, the Army Central Sports Club (CSKA), has suffered particularly badly in the 1990s.
It has been split by a row between CSKA sports chief Colonel Alexander Baranovsky and Viktor Tikhonov, who coached the world-beating Soviet sides of the 1980s.

Legal battles have left Tikhonov in charge of a CSKA Moscow team which competes in the top Russian league and in European competition. A separate CSKA team controlled by Baranovsky competes at a lower level.
"The row is hurting both sides, the club and the hockey team. It does no good to Russian hockey, to Tikhonov or to Baranovsky," Sych said.

Tikhonov, a stony-faced former colonel, trained CSKA to 13 consecutive Soviet championships between 1977 and 1990. The Soviet national team led by Tikhonov won one or more major titles almost every year from 1978 and 1990.
Many players and coaches complained about Tikhonov's his iron discipline and tough coaching style.
But Russia last won a world championship in 1993 under coach Boris Mikhailov, who also critisised Tikhonov.
